title: Will at least two of the three comparisons always come out fine?
description: For ten, fifteen and thirty centimetres, two of the three comparisons are fine and one fails. The lengths are put in increasing order to show which comparisons can never fail.
teaching_notes: One idea: with the lengths in increasing order, the comparisons for the two shorter lengths always come out fine, because the longest length is among the other two. Watch for children who check all three comparisons every time.

source: For the lengths 10 cm, 15 cm and 30 cm, two comparisons hold but the third does not. Will there always be at least two comparisons where the direct length is less than the sum of the other two? Consider the lengths in increasing order.
video_script.why: The child has made all three comparisons for a set and now sees which of them can be skipped.
video_script.substitution: The lengths ten, fifteen and thirty centimetres stand for any three lengths written in increasing order.
video_script.anchor: The lengths ten, fifteen and thirty centimetres in increasing order, with three comparisons
video_script.payoff_line: Yes, at least two comparisons always come out fine.

final_answer.value: Yes: only the longest length needs to be checked
final_answer.spoken: yes, at least two comparisons always come out fine, and only the longest length needs to be checked

hold_back: Only the longest length needs to be checked
never_show: the words only the longest length needs to be checked before the answer beat
maths_rules: the other two lengths for the shortest and the middle length include the longest, which is already bigger than either
video_script.design: One idea: when the lengths are in increasing order, the comparisons for the two shorter lengths cannot fail. The three lengths stay in the anchor band; the working band holds the board solution.

beats.on_screen: strips of 10 cm, 15 cm and 30 cm in increasing order; two ticks and one cross; a question mark
beats.colours: ticks in green, cross in red
narration: <bookmark mark='scene'/>This is a question from your book.
<bookmark mark='two'/>For ten, fifteen and thirty centimetres, two comparisons come out fine and one does not.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Will at least two come out fine for any three lengths?

beats.on_screen: the strips and the question mark stay on the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: three lengths with one marked as the direct length and the other two added as the roundabout length

marks.hint: the lengths are arranged in increasing order

beats.colours: direct length in red, roundabout length in yellow
narration: <bookmark mark='three'/>Three lengths give three comparisons.
<bookmark mark='fine'/>A comparison is fine when one length is less than the other two added together.
<bookmark mark='hint'/>The book's hint is to put the lengths in increasing order.

beats.on_screen: Given: 10 cm, 15 cm, 30 cm, in increasing order

marks.given: the three lengths are written in increasing order

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the lengths ten, fifteen and thirty centimetres, in increasing order.

beats.on_screen: To find: will at least two comparisons always come out fine?
narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find which comparisons come out fine, and why.

marks.others: 15 and 30 are added to 45 in yellow

beats.colours: direct length in red, roundabout length in yellow
narration: <bookmark mark='short'/>Step one, the shortest length is ten.
<bookmark mark='others'/>The other two add to fifteen plus thirty, which is forty five.
<bookmark mark='ok'/>The other two include the longest side, which alone is bigger than ten.

marks.others: 10 and 30 are added to 40 in yellow

beats.colours: direct length in red, roundabout length in yellow
narration: <bookmark mark='mid'/>Step two, the middle length is fifteen.
<bookmark mark='others'/>The other two add to ten plus thirty, which is forty.
<bookmark mark='ok'/>Again the longest side is among them, and thirty alone is bigger than fifteen.

marks.others: 10 and 15 are added to 25 in yellow

beats.colours: direct length in red, roundabout length in yellow, the cross in red
narration: <bookmark mark='long'/>Step three, the longest length is thirty.
<bookmark mark='others'/>The other two add to ten plus fifteen, which is twenty five.
<bookmark mark='bad'/>This time the longest side is not among them, and the comparison can fail.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: shorter lengths: the longest side is always among the other two

marks.why: the longest strip is shown inside the sum of the other two for each shorter length

narration: <bookmark mark='why'/>Step four, for each shorter length the longest side is among the other two.
That is why those two comparisons always come out fine.
<bookmark mark='new'/>Step five, check with another set, seven, ten and fifteen.
<bookmark mark='first'/>Seven is less than twenty five, and ten is less than twenty two.
The two shorter lengths come out fine again.

beats.on_screen: Answer: Yes. Only the longest length needs to be checked
narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Yes, at least two comparisons always come out fine.
Only the longest length needs to be checked.
